patient.chief_complaint: Painful right eye visual loss and progressive left leg weakness with urinary urgency over two weeks
patient.history_present_illness:
Ms. Priya Sharma is a 31-year-old right-handed South Asian woman who presents to the neurology inpatient service for evaluation of painful vision loss in her right eye and progressive lower extremity weakness. She was in her usual state of health until approximately 16 days ago, when she developed periorbital pain behind her right eye that worsened with eye movement. Over the following 2 to 3 days, she noticed blurring and central haziness in her right visual field, with difficulty reading text on her computer screen. She initially attributed this to eye strain from her laboratory work and deferred medical attention. The visual symptoms plateaued and remain at roughly the same level over the past 10 days.

Approximately 10 days ago, she began noticing a new sensation of heaviness and stiffness in her left leg, initially subtle but now clearly interfering with her walking. She reports a band-like tightening sensation around her mid-torso at approximately the level of her navel. Over the past week she has developed urinary urgency with one episode of near-incontinence. She endorses intermittent electric shock-like sensations shooting down her spine and into both legs when she flexes her neck, which began about one week ago. She has noticed that her right eye vision worsens transiently after her morning shower, returning to baseline after several minutes.

Her husband brought her to the emergency department yesterday after she stumbled while walking and he observed her left foot dragging. In the emergency department an urgent brain MRI was performed; she is now admitted to the neurology service for further evaluation and workup.

On direct questioning, she recalls a brief episode of blurry vision in her right eye approximately three years ago lasting about one week that was attributed to fatigue by her general practitioner. She did not receive an ophthalmologic evaluation at that time and the episode resolved spontaneously. She denies prior limb weakness, paresthesias, bowel dysfunction, fever, oral ulcers, skin rash, joint pains, hiccups, nausea, or vomiting. She has no known personal or family history of autoimmune or demyelinating disease. She is planning to start a family in the coming years and is very concerned about treatment implications.

results.title: International consensus diagnostic criteria for neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorders
results.authors: Wingerchuk DM, Banwell B, Bennett JL, et al.
results.summary: NMOSD diagnosis requires AQP4-IgG seropositivity with at least one core clinical characteristic (optic neuritis, acute myelitis, area postrema syndrome, acute brainstem syndrome, symptomatic narcolepsy/diencephalic syndrome, or symptomatic cerebral syndrome). In AQP4-IgG seronegative NMOSD, at least two core characteristics are required plus additional MRI criteria including longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis (LETM, spanning ≥3 contiguous vertebral segments). Short (<2 vertebral segment) peripheral cord lesions are not a feature of AQP4+ NMOSD and favor MS.

results.title: Diagnosis of MOG antibody-associated disease: International MOGAD Panel proposed criteria
results.authors: Banwell B, Bennett JL, Marignier R, et al.
results.summary: MOGAD requires MOG-IgG positivity (cell-based assay, which has higher specificity than ELISA) plus a compatible clinical syndrome (optic neuritis, transverse myelitis, ADEM, or cerebral cortical encephalitis). MOGAD optic neuritis is often bilateral, anterior, with disc edema; MOGAD myelitis often involves the conus; MOGAD is not associated with Dawson fingers, black holes, or periventricular lesions in the typical MS distribution. CSF oligoclonal bands are typically absent in MOGAD (present in <10% of cases).

results.title: Diagnosis of multiple sclerosis: 2017 revisions of the McDonald criteria
results.authors: Thompson AJ, Banwell BL, Barkhof F, et al.
results.summary: McDonald 2017 criteria require DIS and DIT. CSF-specific oligoclonal bands (≥2, CSF-restricted) can substitute for DIT when DIS is demonstrated. MS spinal lesions are typically short-segment, peripheral, and dorsolateral; contrast with NMOSD's longitudinally extensive central cord lesions.

output.summary: The clinical triad of optic neuritis, myelitis, and area postrema syndrome raises the differential of NMOSD versus MOGAD versus MS. Key discriminators: (1) AQP4-IgG by cell-based assay (high sensitivity/specificity for NMOSD) — negative result substantially lowers but does not eliminate probability of NMOSD; (2) MOG-IgG by cell-based assay — required for MOGAD diagnosis; negative result with negative AQP4-IgG in a patient with Dawson fingers, periventricular lesions, black holes, and CSF oligoclonal bands favors MS; (3) Cord lesion length — LETM (≥3 segments) favors NMOSD; short, eccentric peripheral lesion (<2 segments) favors MS; (4) CSF OCB — present in approximately 85-95% of MS, typically absent in NMOSD and MOGAD (<10%). This distinction is management-critical: several MS disease-modifying therapies (particularly natalizumab and certain other immunotherapies) may worsen NMOSD.

sequence_constraints.reason: Brain MRI should precede lumbar puncture to confirm absence of mass effect or herniation risk before LP

critical_actions: Send AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG by cell-based assay (not ELISA) — these results are load-bearing for the MS vs. NMOSD/MOGAD distinction and must be obtained before committing to DMT
Measure cord lesion length on spine MRI — short eccentric cord lesion (<2 vertebral segments) argues against LETM of NMOSD; document the lesion craniocaudal extent explicitly
Characterize the brain MRI lesion pattern — Dawson-finger periventricular lesions, juxtacortical involvement, callososeptal lesions, and black holes are typical of MS and atypical for NMOSD/MOGAD
Establish the MS vs. NMOSD/MOGAD diagnosis BEFORE initiating DMT — natalizumab and some other MS DMTs can cause catastrophic neurological worsening in NMOSD
Treat acute relapse with high-dose IV methylprednisolone (1 g daily for 3-5 days); consider plasma exchange for steroid-refractory severe relapse affecting vision or ambulation
Check JC virus antibody index before considering natalizumab; assess vaccination status before B-cell depleting or S1P-modulator therapy
Discuss family planning with patient before DMT selection — teriflunomide is teratogenic; interferon-beta and glatiramer have the most periconception safety data
Supplement vitamin D to adequate levels (target 25-OH Vitamin D >40 ng/mL)
contraindicated_actions: Do not diagnose or treat as NMOSD solely on the basis of the clinical syndrome (optic neuritis plus myelitis) without antibody and MRI lesion-length data — the workup here excludes NMOSD
Do not initiate natalizumab or fingolimod in a patient with possible or confirmed NMOSD — these agents are associated with severe neurological worsening and rebound attacks in NMOSD

Do not interpret the low-positive ANA (1:80 homogeneous) as diagnostic of lupus CNS disease or redirect workup toward SLE without further supporting features — low-titer ANA is common in the general population and does not alter the MS diagnosis here
Do not start teriflunomide in this woman of childbearing potential who plans pregnancy within two years — teratogenic with prolonged hepatic elimination half-life
Do not omit spinal cord MRI — cord lesion length is the single most discriminating MRI feature between MS and NMOSD and must be measured
Do not use ELISA-based AQP4 or MOG antibody assays — these have higher false-negative rates than cell-based assays; a negative ELISA does not exclude NMOSD or MOGAD
Do not use chronic oral corticosteroids as long-term MS disease-modifying therapy — they are ineffective for relapse prevention and carry significant harm
key_reasoning_points: Optic neuritis plus myelitis is the signature presentation of NMOSD and MOGAD — both must be actively excluded with cell-based antibody assays before diagnosing RRMS, because the treatment implications differ substantially (certain MS DMTs worsen NMOSD)

AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG negative by cell-based assay substantially lower (but do not eliminate) probability of NMOSD/MOGAD; the diagnosis is resolved by the totality of findings: Dawson-finger brain MRI pattern, short eccentric cord lesion, and CSF OCB positive — all three converge on MS

Cord lesion length is the critical MRI discriminator: NMOSD characteristically produces longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis (≥3 contiguous vertebral segments, central, often enhancing); MS cord lesions are short-segment (<2 vertebral segments), eccentric, and peripheral — this patient's single T6-T7 lesion spanning 11 mm argues decisively against LETM

CSF oligoclonal bands are present in approximately 85-95% of MS patients and typically absent in NMOSD (<15%) and MOGAD (<10%) — CSF-restricted OCB positive in this patient is concordant with MS and further discriminates against NMOSD/MOGAD

The low-positive ANA (1:80) is a red herring: low-titer ANA is present in 5-15% of healthy individuals and does not support lupus CNS disease; the MS workup findings are internally consistent and the ANA does not alter the diagnosis

the 2024 revised McDonald criteria are satisfied: DIS is established by lesions in four MS-typical regions (periventricular, juxtacortical, infratentorial, cord); DIT is established by simultaneous enhancing and non-enhancing lesions on the same scan AND by CSF-restricted OCB; RRMS diagnosis is secure

Tier per the July 2026 clinical review: McDonald 2024: dissemination in space and time is established on MRI, and oligoclonal bands substitute for dissemination in time rather than being required — the reviewers' point.

July 2026 review applied end to end: brain and cervical/thoracic cord MRI use an MS protocol; CSF is conditional, never mandatory; OCT/VEP and AQP4/MOG testing answer selected optic or atypical questions rather than forming a blanket panel.

The 2024 revised McDonald framework recognizes the optic nerve as a fifth topography and accepts the kappa free-light-chain index as an alternative positive-CSF marker; these additions do not make optic testing or lumbar puncture universal.

red_herrings.data_point: Optic neuritis plus acute myelitis — the clinical phenotype of the current relapse
red_herrings.intended_effect: The combination of optic neuritis and myelitis is the hallmark NMOSD presentation and may anchor a naive agent toward an AQP4 disorder, prompting consideration of NMOSD-directed treatment before antibody and MRI lesion-length data are available
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Optic neuritis plus myelitis is the entry point into the differential — not a diagnosis. The complete workup (AQP4-IgG negative by CBA, MOG-IgG negative by CBA, short eccentric cord lesion <2 segments, typical Dawson-finger brain MRI, CSF OCB positive) excludes NMOSD and MOGAD and establishes RRMS

red_herrings.intended_effect: A positive ANA may redirect the agent toward CNS lupus or overlap autoimmune syndrome, broadening the differential inappropriately or prompting additional lupus-specific testing that delays definitive diagnosis
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: ANA at 1:80 homogeneous pattern is a low titer present in 5-15% of healthy individuals; it lacks specificity at this level and is not supported by other lupus features (no rash, no arthritis, no renal involvement, normal complement, normal ESR/CRP). It does not alter the MS diagnosis.
